title: Knowledge Check 12 - Lessons 56-61
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 56-61 - Governance and Observability | Multi-Agent Orchestration. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: Escalation Rate rose overall, and a breakdown shows the increase is concentrated in one intent. Which capability produced that localization?
options: The Trust dimension tab
The Usage dimension tab
The Session Outcome stack bar chart
Performance Insights, which breaks a metric down by subagent, intent, or action
questions.explanation: Performance Insights provides the per-subagent, per-intent, and per-action breakdowns that localize a trend before you open sessions.

questions.question: A session failed and you must tell a failing external action apart from a bad retrieval. Where do you look?
options: The Effectiveness tab, which shows the rates
The Trace tab, which shows the time-ordered steps with per-step timing and error text
The filter bar, which scopes the dashboard
The saves views menu, which stores your columns
questions.explanation: Trace lists every processing step with its timing and any error text, which is what separates a failing action from a slow or wrong retrieval.

questions.question: A filter returns no results for a session you know happened. Which explanation fits?
options: The session exceeded the default two hour timeout and was deleted
The agent has more than one active version
Its intent is an untagged instance that did not join a cluster, so it does not appear in the session trace
The agent was deactivated at the time of the session
questions.explanation: Untagged intents do not appear in the session trace even though the session holds them, so a low-volume intent can be missing from the trace view.

questions.question: An agent routes every returns request correctly to the Returns subagent, but the replies are too terse and miss detail the customer asked for. The Trace shows no errors. Which lever do you change?
options: The subagent's instructions, because the routing is correct and the answer quality is the problem
The topic scope, because the request should route elsewhere
The action inputs, because a step failed
The knowledge source, because retrieval returned nothing
questions.explanation: Correct routing with weak answers points at the instructions, while a failing step or wrong retrieval would point at actions or knowledge instead.

questions.question: A request never reaches the subagent that owns it, and the agent answers from a different topic instead. The answer text is otherwise fine. Which lever do you change?
options: The instructions of the wrong subagent, because its wording is off
The alert thresholds, because the metric breached a level
The topic scope, by adding or clarifying a subagent so the router selects the right one
The dashboard filters, because the report is scoped incorrectly
questions.explanation: A misrouted request with a fine answer is a classification and scope problem, which you fix by clarifying the subagent that should own it.

questions.question: Success Rate drops and the Trace shows an error step where an action fails for some users. Which statement best explains it?
options: The agent's instructions are too vague and need rewriting
The action fails at run time because it runs under each user's security context, so check the action's inputs and permissions
The knowledge article behind the action is out of date
The metric is lagging and the drop is not real
questions.explanation: An error step in an action points at the action and its inputs, and because actions run under the running user's security context a missing permission fails them at run time.

questions.question: A single agent's instruction block has grown until it invokes the wrong Subagent for billing requests, even though every Subagent is correctly scoped. Which wall has it hit?
options: A data boundary limit, because billing data lives in another system
Domain specialisation collapse, where the larger instruction block reduces routing precision
A licensing limit on the number of Actions
A hard limit on the number of Subagents per agent
questions.explanation: Domain specialisation collapse is the named wall where an agent that tries to be an expert in everything applies the wrong logic, and routing precision falls as the instruction block grows.

questions.question: In Agentforce Builder you connect a specialist agent to an orchestrator. Which artifact governs when the orchestrator delegates to that subagent?
options: The subagent's record type
The orchestrator's version number
The subagent's assigned profile
The connected subagent's description, set in Basic Information
questions.explanation: The description on the connected subagent governs the orchestrator's delegation decision, which is why a vague description produces unreliable routing.

questions.question: In a single-org multi-agent design, which agent can escalate a conversation to a human?
options: Only the orchestrator agent
Only the connected subagent that owns the record
Any agent in the design
An escalation agent added as an extra subagent
questions.explanation: Only the orchestrator agent can escalate to a human, so human handoff is centralised at the front door rather than handled by connected subagents.

questions.question: Sales and support both read the same account records and call the same Flows. The support team asks for its own agent. Following the single-versus-multi-agent decision, what is the better answer?
options: Keep one agent and add a support Subagent with its Actions
Split into two agents and connect them with an orchestrator
Split into two agents and use A2A between them
Move the support team to a different Salesforce org
questions.explanation: When the process shares one data boundary and one domain, the decision framework favours a single agent with a new Subagent and its Actions rather than a new agent and an orchestrator.

questions.question: A team splits a working single agent into an orchestrator and three specialists. Which outcome should they expect?
options: Lower latency because the specialists work in parallel
Lower cost per turn because each agent does less
Higher latency and higher cost per turn because each agent runs its own reasoning loop and orchestration adds a hop
Unchanged latency and cost
questions.explanation: Each agent runs its own reasoning loop and orchestration adds a hop, so splitting raises latency and the number of model calls behind one user message.

questions.question: Which situation genuinely justifies splitting a single agent into multi-agent orchestration?
options: The requirement spans two business topics
The instruction block is long but still routes correctly
The team wants a tidier architecture diagram
The needed data, workflows, and permissions live in a different Salesforce org
questions.explanation: A data boundary wall, where the needed data and permissions live in a different org or system, is one of the named walls that earns the architectural change, while topic count and tidiness do not.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Model Context Protocol in an agent architecture?
options: To let agents delegate tasks to peer agents across vendors
To replace the agent's reasoning engine
To connect agents to external tools, data sources, and APIs through a standard tool interface
To store conversation history outside the org
questions.explanation: MCP is the open standard that exposes external capabilities as callable tools an agent can discover and invoke, while delegation to peer agents belongs to A2A.

questions.question: Which statement about the Agent-to-Agent Protocol is correct?
options: It is an open protocol for agent-to-agent communication, and Salesforce was a founding member alongside Google, Microsoft, SAP, and AWS
It is a Salesforce proprietary protocol for in-org subagents
It is a tool interface that exposes external APIs as callable actions
It is a data store for Agentforce reasoning traces
questions.explanation: A2A is an open, cross-vendor protocol for peer agent communication, and Salesforce was a founding member of the effort, so it is not a proprietary or tool-level construct.

questions.question: A remote system owns part of the reasoning and planning for a task and should be delegated a sub-task as a peer. Which protocol fits?
options: MCP, because it exposes tools
MCP, because it carries Agent Cards
Neither protocol applies to delegation
A2A, because the remote thing is used as a collaborating agent rather than as a tool
questions.explanation: The rule of thumb is that a remote capability is reached with MCP and a remote agent that owns part of the reasoning is delegated to with A2A.

questions.question: What does the Agent-to-Agent Protocol carry on the wire to enable discovery?
options: A tool contract with callable function signatures
An Agent Card, a machine-readable description of the agent's capabilities
A record type and a permission set
A Flow version and its actions
questions.explanation: A2A has agents publish an Agent Card that describes their capabilities so peers can discover and invoke them, while a tool contract with callable signatures is MCP.

questions.question: Which statement contrasts the two protocols correctly?
options: MCP delegates to a peer that reasons, and A2A exposes tools
Both protocols delegate to peer agents
Both protocols expose external tools
MCP exposes tools and context, while A2A delegates to a peer agent that owns part of the planning
questions.explanation: The contrast is exposure versus delegation: MCP gives the agent new hands through tools and context, while A2A gives it a colleague that owns part of the reasoning.

questions.question: An Agentforce agent must reach an external system that is not MCP-enabled. What does the documented architecture use to expose it?
options: MuleSoft acts as an MCP wrapper that exposes the API as MCP tools
A2A Agent Cards are generated automatically for the API
The agent calls the native API directly with no wrapper
A connected subagent replaces the external system
questions.explanation: Where a remote system is not MCP-enabled, MuleSoft acts as an MCP wrapper that exposes those APIs as MCP tools, which is why the missing wrapper blocks the call.
